title: With Due Respect (Vol. 6) -- Ch. 1: Destiny and Aspiration
primary_topics: Chapter 1 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 6) -- CJP's September 6, 2009 Inquirer column handicapping the 2010 presidential race through Ninoy Aquino's old maxim that one can aspire for and win a Senate seat 'but the presidency? That's destiny'

His 'destiny' thread -- how brilliant aspirants (Recto, Doy Laurel, Gerardo Roxas, Salonga, Ninoy himself) never reached Malacañang, while the 'reluctant' Cory and now her son Noynoy were 'propelled' to it after his mother's death turned Mar Roxas into Noynoy's endorser

His 'succession' thread -- vice presidents Quirino, Garcia and Arroyo who rose 'at the right place at the right time,' illustrated by Romulo's declined VP slot, Arsenio Lacson's quip about a VP's job, and GMA settling for the vice presidency in 1998

His 'ambition' thread -- the meticulous planners Macapagal and Marcos, and now Manuel Villar's 'sipag at tiyaga' climb -- closing with a 'battle royale' forecast among Noynoy, Erap, Villar and Noli de Castro, and the maxim 'better to win as VP than to lose as president'
sub_topics: The organizing maxim: at a 1971 press conference, Ninoy Aquino -- then the Liberal Party's senatorial campaign manager -- said one can 'aspire for, plan and win a seat in the Senate,' but the presidency is 'destiny'

Destiny denied and bestowed: 'brilliant officials' like Claro Recto, Doy Laurel, Gerardo Roxas, Jovito Salonga and Ninoy himself 'aspired and certainly deserved' the presidency but never reached it, while the 'unpretentious, guileless, and reluctant' Cory was 'propelled' to it -- and now her son Noynoy, another 'reluctant presidentiable'

The altered plan: Noynoy had pledged to back Mar Roxas, but Cory's death 'altered their best-laid plans,' and Mar, recognizing 'the changed landscape,' 'unconditionally endorsed Noynoy as the Liberal Party standard-bearer'

Other destinies: Ramos pursued the presidency only when he feared for the Edsa legacy and, though 'rebuffed by the ruling party,' won 'with Cory's help'; Estrada, content as 'king of San Juan' until his Edsa ouster, was on 'a new journey to regain his destiny' despite the legal clouds of being a former convict and (allegedly) a constitutionally barred former president

Succession's accidents: VPs Quirino, Garcia and Arroyo 'ascended because they were at the right place at the right time' -- Romulo had declined Roxas's VP offer (preferring the US ambassadorship), so Quirino inherited the mantle on Roxas's 1948 death; and Garcia took over when Magsaysay died in 1957

Lacson's quip: declining Magsaysay's VP nomination, Manila Mayor Arsenio Lacson joked that 'a vice-president's job is to wait for the president to die' and that the healthy Magsaysay 'would make a healthier president' -- only for Garcia, not Lacson, to succeed

The planners: Macapagal and Marcos (both 'bar topnotchers') 'meticulously planned their way' to power, a road Manuel Villar now travels under 'sipag at tiyaga' -- from the speakership to the Senate presidency -- having been recruited into the Nacionalista Party at Doy Laurel's deathbed wish and risen 'to the top of the latest surveys'

The forecast: CJP predicts a 2010 'battle royale' among Noynoy ('the yellow man of destiny'), Erap ('the resurgent hero of the masa'), Villar ('the epitome of logistics and planning') and Noli de Castro (Arroyo and Lakas-Kampi-CMD's choice), with also-rans likely to 'slide down to the VP derby' -- since it is 'better to win as VP than to lose as president'

notable_anecdotes: Ninoy's maxim: CJP anchors the column on Ninoy Aquino's 1971 line that the Senate can be won, but the presidency is 'destiny.'

Lacson's quip: he relays Arsenio Lacson's joke that a VP merely waits 'for the president to die,' and that the healthy Magsaysay 'would make a healthier president' -- before Garcia, not Lacson, succeeded.
Romulo's declined slot: he notes Carlos Romulo turned down Roxas's VP offer to be US ambassador, leaving Quirino to inherit the presidency in 1948.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 1 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 6), CJP's September 6, 2009 Inquirer column, handicaps the looming 2010 presidential race through Ninoy Aquino's old maxim that one can 'aspire for, plan and win a seat in the Senate' but the presidency is 'destiny.' Under 'destiny,' he notes that deserving aspirants -- Recto, Doy Laurel, Gerardo Roxas, Salonga, Ninoy himself -- never reached Malacañang, while the 'unpretentious... and reluctant' Cory was 'propelled' to it, and now her son Noynoy, another 'reluctant presidentiable,' was catapulted after Cory's death 'altered' his plan to back Mar Roxas (who then 'unconditionally endorsed' him). Ramos pursued the presidency only to save the Edsa legacy, and Estrada -- once 'king of San Juan' -- was on 'a new journey to regain his destiny' despite legal clouds over a former convict and a former president running again. Under 'succession,' VPs Quirino, Garcia and Arroyo rose 'at the right place at the right time' (Romulo having declined Roxas's VP slot for the US ambassadorship, and Arsenio Lacson having quipped that a VP merely waits 'for the president to die'). Under 'ambition,' the planners Macapagal and Marcos -- both bar topnotchers -- 'meticulously planned their way,' a road Manuel Villar now travels under 'sipag at tiyaga,' having been recruited into the Nacionalista Party at Doy Laurel's deathbed wish. CJP forecasts a 'battle royale' among Noynoy ('the yellow man of destiny'), Erap ('the resurgent hero of the masa'), Villar ('the epitome of logistics and planning') and Noli de Castro (Arroyo's choice), with also-rans likely to 'slide down to the VP derby' -- since it is 'better to win as VP than to lose as president.'
